articles.title: Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy
articles.author: Oren Etzioni
paras: The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.
A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.
Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

The window is closing . Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Competitors are everywhere . AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”

The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.
Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

Jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

At AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”

Finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook says Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”

Prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”

Swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction company I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.
Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, said it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one big shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

To repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one says, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.
In AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

articles.title: Seattle Social Housing Developer Drops Design Director
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Michael Eliason, Director of Design & Policy at the Seattle Social Housing Developer (SSHD), departed that role last month in a personnel move that signals a strategic pivot for a public development authority still finding its footing. Eliason's former position will no longer exist, with the SSHD instead planning to hire a Director of Policy with a different portfolio of work.

Seattle voters created the social housing developer in 2023 by initiative, providing a mandate for the production of mixed-income, permanently affordable housing, operating independently of Seattle City Council or mayoral control. Two years later, voters approved a dedicated funding source for social housing via a high-earners payroll tax , with early revenue dramatically exceeding expectations in a way that has given the SSHD significant forward momentum .

Eliason had been brought on in January, after being closely involved in advocacy around Seattle's two social housing initiatives. Prior to becoming staff, he had served as one of the developer's first board members, an appointment made via members of Seattle's Green New Deal Oversight Board. Eliason's influence was credited with mandates for Passivhaus design being incorporated into the developer's mission from the jump.

Passivhaus standards create buildings that are highly energy efficient, using thermal insulation, airtightness, and filtered ventilation. While more expensive at the outset, the design creates cost savings as energy costs are reduced, with a benefit of providing more comfortable interior spaces that are more climate-friendly at the same time.

As a strong evangelist for Passivhaus standards and improved urban design, Eliason has pushed for green building requirements for social housing as a contributor for The Urbanist as well as in a book titled Building for People .

Eliason exited the developer just as it has appeared to hit its stride, announcing its first new construction project in the Central District and its second building acquisition in Delridge in the span of just a few weeks. After the SSHD board replaced its initial pick for CEO, Roberto Jimenez, with Interim CEO Tiffani McCoy – who had led the push for social housing in Seattle as co-founder of the advocacy group House Our Neighbors – things appeared to fall into place.
More social housing projects are expected to be announced soon, with a goal of owning 1,000 units by the end of 2027 and putting more in the construction pipeline.
In a post on LinkedIn made shortly after his departure, Eliason characterized the decision as a pivot away from an emphasis on design in future social housing buildings in Seattle.

"I recently learned that design would no longer be a priority for the Seattle Social Housing Developer, as they eliminated the Director of Design & Policy position," Eliason wrote. "It was an exciting run, and I am proud of the work I accomplished with the nearly three-year effort on the board, and then transitioning to staff. This work included massive efforts around standing up the real estate committee and working on the strategic plan - to finding viable and high quality parcels (not on arterials!), steering procurement efforts with architecture firms, working on legislative and local land use policies to deliver more/better/cost effective housing, and adding new construction values - all of which would go on to inform the design standards for new housing."

But sources familiar with how operations at the developer have disputed his characterization, instead pointing to a shift that has occurred as the SSHD has been navigating rules around public procurement for construction projects. Earlier this year, the SSHD rolled out a roster of design firms that will be considered for future developments, including CAST Architecture, Neiman Taber, Mithun, Schemata Workshop, and Perkins Eastman.

With those firms handling the bulk of design work, the SSHD does have less of a need for in-house design expertise, but did recently bring on Jacqui Aiello, former architectural designer at SMR Architecture, a firm focused on affordable housing. Aiello's hire cuts against the assertion that the developer is de-prioritizing design work.

"The Seattle Social Housing Developer made a sincere effort to keep Michael Eliason on staff by providing him with several options," SSHD Director of Communications Lilly Ana Fowler told The Urbanist. "We wish him the best with future endeavors and sincerely thank him for all his contributions to social housing. SSHD takes design seriously and is working with a number of architecture firms on both small and large social housing projects that prioritize family-sized housing, Passive House standards, open spaces and Universal Design."
Eliason did not respond to a request for comment from The Urbanist for this story.

The new Director of Policy position will be tasked with advocating for legislative changes to make it easier to build social housing in Seattle, and with representing the developer in front of governmental authorities, including the Seattle City Council. Rather than leading the design team, the role will be focused on translating "technical legal and regulatory ideas into clear, compelling information for audiences ranging from elected officials and agency staff to community members, the Board, and the media," according to a job posting from this month.

articles.title: Capitol Hill’s Station 7 passes the keys to a new owner ahead of a new season on 15th Ave E
articles.author: CHS
paras: The building’s old firehouse gates had to be removed earlier this year (Image: Station 7)

Jamie Marcello was not expecting to take over Capitol Hill boutique Station 7 this year. But after Mary Jensen , long-time owner of the 11-year-old locally-sourced gift shop and its online store, announced she was ready to pass the baton, Marcello was ready to accept the responsibility in keeping the small business alive.

Station 7 has a tradition of passing down the keys to its 15th Ave E shop. The small business was started by Danielle Tilden who passed it down to her daughter Lauren . And after working alongside Tilden for years, Jensen now holds the keys to the shop housed in a long ago Capitol Hill fire station.
“[There has been] so much learning that’s been happening between myself and Mary,” Marcello said about the first few weeks navigating the logistical and financial aspects of transferring ownership.
Although this is Marcello’s first ownership role, she said Jensen has been walking beside her every step of the way. “She’s a great mentor. She wants me to succeed.”
Marcello was first introduced to Station 7 as a Seattle University student, when she worked on a project to encourage more engagement between students and small businesses.

From there, she worked intermittently during college, alternating between full- or part-time and occasionally filling in the gaps when the store needed extra hands. She said throughout the years, she “kind of grew along with the shop.”
“This is a shop that’s been so important to me for such a long part of my life,” Marcello said. “I just felt like, wow, this is such a unique, exciting opportunity. I can’t wait to jump in.”

In 2025 , Station 7 posted an “honest overview” detailing its revenue, expenses, and profit margin. The infographic reads, “To be honest, this year so far has been really tough. We’re losing a lot more than we’re making: just over 2.5x more, actually.”

For many small businesses, owners see an influx in revenue during the holiday season, which Marcello said can come with its own pressure to hit the goals and sales needed to budget for the upcoming year.

But running a small business is “always a risk,” Marcello said. There is also the long path for this era of 15th Ave small businesses to navigate as the neighborhood awaits a massive redevelopment in the heart of the commercial strip right next door to Station 7.
Earlier this year, Ada’s Technical Books closed after its 16-year-long run .
In September , CHS reported the shuttering of three 15th Ave establishments: Rione XIII , Rubinstein Bagels , and Bar Vacilando due to building and landlord issues.
Now, the darkened businesses’ empty windows face Station 7 and Marcello said she feels the weight of their absence.

“Even going into the shop the other day, I was really excited. I was like, ‘Wow, I got a parking spot so easily, this never happens,’” Marcello said. “And then I had to sit with that and then realize, ‘Oh, that’s because people aren’t really on the street as much anymore.’”

Station 7, the gift shop, resides in Capitol Hill’s historic Fire Station 7 which was built in 1920, decommissioned a few decades later, and revived in 1970 by the community-based, architectural and design firm, Environmental Works or EWorks.
EWorks has owned and operated out of the firehouse since the 70s, providing architectural and urban planning services to primarily under-served communities and organizations across Washington.
Marcello said it has been “very reassuring” to know the firm is taking care of upkeep on the more than 100-year-old building, taking the responsibility off her shoulders and into safe hands.

“We love the building. We love where we’re at,” Marcello said, with no current plans to move or do any major renovations. “We really want, in this transition, for people and customers to walk in and still feel very much familiar in the same place that they’ve been going to.”
Station 7 opened in the building in the summer of 2015 — before that, the space was home to the last video rental shop on Capitol Hill , On 15th Video .

That is the past. The future is coming. Station 7 is lined up to get somewhere around 172 new neighbors in one of the biggest changes ever for the street in a six-story redevelopment of the old QFC and parking lot just north of the old firehouse.

In Station 7’s more immediate future, Marcello encourages customers to treat holiday shopping like it is “voting with your dollars,” a motto she heard from a fellow local business enthusiast and carries with her.

“As people want life to be more and more convenient, people are sometimes stepping away from more intentional buying,” Marcello said. Station 7 prides itself on sourcing local and handmade goods, with over 70% of its in-shop products belonging to local, women-owned businesses, according to its website.
“I’m definitely hopeful that people will continue to see the value in buying from makers in our community.”
Marcello also said she is in the process of setting up various workshops for the upcoming winter months, including an upcycled gift wrapping event and inviting a watercolor artist to host a class.

Station 7 will also join 15th Ave businesses in the second annual Capitol Hill Holiday Wine Walk on December 9 , which Marcello said “will just be another really fun moment for the neighborhood to come together.”
To stay updated on Station 7 news or upcoming events, visit its Instagram or station7seattle.com .

articles.title: Pikes/Pines | A quiet night on 19th Ave E for two of Capitol Hill’s wild neighbors
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Thanks to neighbor Randy for sharing this 19th Ave E scene
A neighbor in the CHS Facebook Group shared this otherworldly scene of urban nature from Capitol HIll’s 19th Ave E — a mother and child making their way through the city on a drizzling autumn night.

CHS has noted our cervine neighbors here and there over the years. In 2023, the Seattle Parks Department told us that deer that took up residency in Volunteer Park that summer were welcome to stay as long as they wanted .

As this Pikes/Pines essay from that summer shared, Black-tailed Deer (*Odocoileus hemionus columbianus*), a subspecies of Mule Deer, are residents on Capitol Hill, making appearances in green spaces like Volunteer Park and Interlaken Park .

Unlike populations that migrate long distances, some urban deer thrive locally because parks and greenbelts provide year-round forage along sunlit forest edges and shelter far from predators like cougars. Requiring a relatively small territory, they adapt to dense city pockets.

Deer that weren’t born in Seattle typically arrive like the rest of us — through juvenile dispersal. Usually young bucks push out to establish new territories, moving gradually inward from surrounding suburbs like Shoreline, Renton, and Burien. To bypass busy highways and dense commercial zones, they follow ribbons of natural cover such as steep wooded ravines, creek drainages, overgrown railroad corridors, and power-line right-of-ways that link suburban forests to city parks. Because Black-tailed deer are strong swimmers, they also navigate along riverbanks like the Duwamish, traverse Puget Sound beaches at low tide, and even swim across channels like the Lake Washington Ship Canal to reach isolated greenbelts, covering the final residential blocks under the cover of darkness.

Dispersing deer reach an area like Interlaken Park by following Seattle’s network of lakeside wetlands, ravines, and greenbelts rather than crossing the dense downtown grid. From the south, they can travel along the Lake Washington shoreline through parks like Seward and Frink into the Washington Park Arboretum , then make a short nighttime crossing into Interlaken. From the north, deer dispersing down wooded ravines like Ravenna Park can swim across the Montlake Cut from Union Bay straight into the Arboretum, or follow vegetated I-5 and Portage Bay embankments through Lake View Cemetery and Volunteer Park.

Once inside the Interlaken–Arboretum–Volunteer Park triangle, surrounding highways and dense city blocks act as a barrier, turning the greenbelt into a self-contained urban forest where arriving deer stay put.

Biologically, these ruminants are well-equipped for Seattle, using a tough upper dental pad to pull vegetation and a four-chambered stomach to ferment high-fiber foods like leaves, fruit, and lichen. When threatened, they can sprint up to 40 mph, leap high fences, or escape using a bouncing gait known as pronking. Because they are primarily active at dawn and dusk, they often go unnoticed.
If you see them, appreciate their presence while maintaining a safe, respectful distance. And snap a picture or two to share with the neighborhood.

This edition of Saturday Night Live opens at the CIA headquarters. In the wake of the Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepping down after details of his extramarital affairs, including one with an accused Chinese spy, came to light, the agency has called together a meeting of the nation’s top tech billionaires: creepy Peter Thiel (James Austin Johnson), robotic Sam Altman (Ben Marshall), awkward Dario Amodei (Jane Wickline), and the insufferable duo of Mark Zuckerberg (Andy Dismukes) and Elon Musk (Jeremy Culhane).

An agent (tonight’s host, John Mulaney) attempts to school them on how not to get honeypotted. Per a helpful Venn diagram: “On this side we have beautiful women, and on this side we have people who would be interested in your shared opinions and interests. I cannot stress this enough: there is no overlap.” He fails to get through to the group (especially the middle-school-like Musk, whom he sprays with water to keep on track), so he hands things over to Jensen “Hide Your Wife” Haung himself, played by a returning Bowen Yang. articles.title: Reclaiming Mary Cassatt: putting overlooked American artist back at heart of impressionism
articles.author: Kim Willsher in Paris
paras: New exhibition restores painter’s place as leading figure in French movement that revolutionised art

As a painter, friend, and collaborator of Edgar Degas, who exhibited with impressionist artists including Claude Monet and Camille Pissarro, Mary Cassatt was at the heart of the 19th-century movement that emerged in France and revolutionised art.

She was also a woman and foreign – “American, American through and through” is how she described herself. As a result, in the 100 years since her death, Cassatt has been frequently overlooked in the country where she produced her best work.

articles.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
articles.author: Tim Dowling
paras: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma?

Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout.
“I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?”

articles.title: Prostate cancer testing now urged for men in their 50s and 60s – a lead author of the new screening guidelines explains why
articles.author:
<name>Andrew Wolf, Professor Emeritus of Medicine, University of Virginia</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/andrew-wolf-2768776"/>
paras: The American Cancer Society announced on Nov. 12, 2026, that it has released major changes to its prostate cancer screening guidelines to improve detection and treatment of the disease.
The Conversation asked Dr. Andrew Wolf , a physician at the University of Virginia who was one of the lead authors of the new guidelines , to walk readers through the changes and why they were made.

The biggest change is that we are making a proactive recommendation to screen for prostate cancer . Previously, we recommended that people talk with their healthcare provider to decide whether or not screening is right for them.
Our new recommendations vary by age and by a person’s risk of developing prostate cancer.

For people at average risk of developing prostate cancer, we recommend they be screened with the prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, blood test every two years from age 50 through 69. PSA is a protein that prostate cells make. Cancer and other conditions can cause PSA levels to rise.

People at higher risk, including Black men and men with a strong family history of prostate cancer, should be screened annually from age 45 to 69. A strong family history means having a family member who was diagnosed with prostate cancer before age 65, or multiple family members diagnosed at any age. People with a single family member diagnosed at age 65 or older should be screened every two years from age 45 years to age 69 years.

For people ages 70 to 74, we recommend they talk with their healthcare provider about whether or not to continue screening. Because there is uncertainty about the benefit of screening for people in this age group, decision-making around screening depends on their personal preferences, overall health status and life expectancy.

For those over age 74, we recommend against prostate cancer screening. The potential harms of screening, such as more invasive follow-up tests and treatment, are likely to exceed the benefits for people in this age group.

Finally, we recommend against using a digital rectal exam to screen for prostate cancer, as it is less effective than the PSA test . The digital rectal exam may still be helpful when further evaluating elevated PSA levels or symptoms related to the prostate gland.
The past decade has seen mounting evidence supporting the benefits of using the PSA blood test to screen for prostate cancer.
The ability of the PSA test to reduce the risk of death from prostate cancer or of being diagnosed with metastatic disease are actually greater than researchers previously thought.

At the same time, there have been significant developments to reduce the potential harms associated with prostate cancer screening, including false positive PSA test results and diagnosis and treatment of prostate tumors that are unlikely to harm patients in the long-term.

Black men have an approximately two-thirds higher risk of developing prostate cancer compared with white men. They are also at greater risk for having more advanced disease at the time of diagnosis. These disparities are likely due to a combination of genetic, environmental, social and healthcare access factors .
Men with a family history of prostate cancer in a close relative – such as a parent, sibling or child – are also at elevated risk.

There are also a number of genetic mutations, such as BRCA2 , that confer significantly elevated risk of prostate cancer. Though screening recommendations for these cases are beyond the scope of our guideline, several professional medical organizations, including the National Comprehensive Cancer Network and the American Urological Association , have issued recommendations for screening people with these high-risk mutations.

For years, clinicians believed that the benefits of PSA screening were uncertain and didn’t necessarily outweigh the potential harms. This stance was in part because of the results of two large prostate cancer screening trials that were published in 2009. One, a U.S. study , found no benefit to screening; the other, a European study , found only a relatively small benefit.

However, it later became clear that the U.S. study was seriously flawed in such a way that it couldn’t have shown a benefit: Almost 90% of the men in the control group – that is, the group that wasn’t supposed to get screened – actually did get screened, and many of the men with abnormal PSA levels didn’t follow-up.

Conversely, most of the men in the European study who were randomized to standard care – no testing – instead of screening did not, in fact, get a PSA test, so it was more of a true comparison of the effect of screening versus not screening.

After researchers followed patients for over two decades in the European study, the effects of screening became clear: Screening reduced the risk of dying from prostate cancer by 13%. And about 500 men needed to be screened to avert one death from prostate cancer.

This may not sound very impressive, but it’s comparable to other routinely offered cancer screening tests, such as mammography for breast cancer . And the proportion of people needing to be screened to save a life would be significantly lower if extrapolated to a lifetime of screening starting at age 45 or 50, rather than the average number of two screenings that men received in the study.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force also has its own prostate cancer screening guidelines. The task force’s guidelines currently recommend that clinicians not screen for prostate cancer unless the patient indicates a preference to proceed. At the time of the task force’s last update in 2018 , it determined that the potential benefits and harms of screening were too closely balanced to recommend screening.
The task force has been in the process of updating those guidelines over the past several years. It is possible that their update will more closely align with that of the American Cancer Society.

I do think we have both sufficient evidence of benefit and sufficient reduction of the risks to now proactively recommend screening. Where the two guidelines do align is that both recommend that patients be informed of the benefits, risks and limitations of prostate cancer screening so they know what they’re getting into.

It is likely that our new screening recommendations will be covered by most insurers. However, patients may have out-of-pocket costs for further testing their doctor orders as a result of an abnormal PSA level.
Even though the benefits far outweigh the risks, there may be legitimate reasons why some people may not wish to undergo screening.

Some people might want to avoid the possibility of needing to get a prostate biopsy , which is how clinicians diagnose prostate cancer if a patient has an elevated PSA and an abnormal follow-up MRI scan or biomarker test. Prostate biopsies are uncomfortable, and they may cause some bleeding or occasionally an infection.

Some people may want to avoid the possibility of needing to undergo active surveillance if they discover they have a tumor that isn’t growing aggressively . Active surveillance involves periodic biopsies, MRI scans or both, which can be inconvenient and anxiety-provoking.
Some people may want to avoid the potential side effects of treating early-stage prostate cancer with surgery or radiation, which can cause sexual, urinary and bowel problems.
Forgoing screening, however, also means forgoing the opportunity to find cancer at its earliest stages, when the chance for a cure is very high.

Andrew Wolf serves as Chair of the American Cancer Society's Guideline Development Group. This is a volunteer position. Opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of the American Cancer Society.

articles.title: Who should run Nvidia? Our picks for Jensen Huang’s successor, whether the board likes it or not
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Nvidia’s board says it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names.

The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Colette Kress , the company’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk said on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang.
The organizers of one, called “ Stand with Jensen ,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees.

The case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment.

Arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU , paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs.
Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported.

He also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the company’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013.

Haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas said in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the New York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.”

One complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi , SoftBank’s AI chip effort launched to compete with Nvidia.
He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public company — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis.

John’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s ouster.

What the betting markets say: On Kalshi , Ian Buck , the Nvidia vice president who created the CUDA software platform, was the favorite at midday Friday. By midday Saturday, Haas had overtaken him, at 25% to Buck’s 18%. Kress was at 10%.

The Axios list of 11 names also includes Apple Executive Chair Tim Cook, for whom President Trump lobbied on Truth Social (“A Legend replaces a Legend!”), along with AMD CEO Lisa Su and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian .

A Northwest wildcard: Analysts have also floated Sanjay Mehrotra , CEO of Boise, Idaho-based Micron Technology, whose memory chips power Nvidia’s AI servers. Mehrotra co-founded SanDisk in 1988 and has run Micron since 2017 .

The AWS chief: Matt Garman has run Amazon Web Services since June 2024, overseeing a business with a $142 billion annual revenue run rate at the end of last year. He started at Amazon as an MBA intern in 2005, joined AWS full time in 2006 as one of its first product managers , and later led its compute business and then its sales and marketing organization.
Another Amazon pick: We’d also look at Peter DeSantis , who now leads a new organization that includes Amazon’s AI models, custom chips and quantum computing, reporting directly to CEO Andy Jassy.

DeSantis joined Amazon as a software developer in 1998. He led the EC2 team from Cape Town, South Africa, through its 2006 launch, and spearheaded Amazon’s 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs, the Israeli chip designer behind its custom silicon.
In 2018, DeSantis unveiled Graviton . In June, he told Bloomberg that AWS was in talks to sell its Trainium AI chips to other companies for their own data centers.
He knows chips, data centers and AI infrastructure at enormous scale. The catch, as John noted: he’s never been a CEO, and the board may want that experience given the circumstances.

The other Amazon name: Dave Treadwell took over AWS compute and machine learning services in August. Treadwell spent 27 years at Microsoft, where he worked on Windows NT, .NET and Xbox and rose to corporate vice president, before joining Amazon in 2016.
The Microsoft bench: On the podcast, Todd ran through a few Microsoft executives who would bring relevant experience:

The insider with Microsoft roots: Nick Parker , a 26-year Microsoft sales veteran, joined Nvidia in August as executive vice president of worldwide field operations, with a pay package worth more than $40 million. He’s new, but he already runs the team that sells Nvidia’s chips to the world’s largest companies.

One more angle: Whoever gets the job will face a growing list of customers trying to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, including Amazon. In his annual shareholder letter in April, Jassy wrote that Amazon’s chips business would have an annual run rate of about $50 billion if it sold chips to AWS and other third parties the way other chipmakers do.
Jassy said it’s “quite possible” Amazon will sell racks of them to third parties in the future.
In a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14, Huang said he hoped his successor was already inside the company. The board has said it will consider both internal and external candidates.
Listen to our full discussion on this week’s GeekWire Podcast .

articles.title: ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote .

Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The company says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

The company said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log . Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user , he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.
In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud.
Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto , a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments ; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption.
In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported , citing Nikkei.

In New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems , including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear . Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”
Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”

The Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours , and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked , it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast .)

Microsoft said Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its users that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.
Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter said he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”
The security company Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”

articles.title: Gov. Ferguson seeks $10M to help develop Eastern Wash. clean-energy hub
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget.
If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park.
“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm.

State officials said General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility , a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors.

In 2024, the Norwegian company Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business , ultimately withdrew its plans.

The Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland.
Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall , but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate.

Ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

articles.title: Alternative Transit Modes
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: As I explained in an earlier guideway post, Sound Transit chose light rail technology to make it easier to use the existing transit tunnel and to run and stop at grade but many new technologies have been developed since. As Sound Transit builds a lot more elevated and tunneled sections and opens new lines in urban areas, it may need to reevaluate that decision. Sound Transit and Metro already use buses, heavy rail (for Sounder), ferries, and trams. Other cities like San Francisco, Mexico, and Paris use even more different modes like people movers and gondolas. In that post I talked about monorail and maglev guiderail systems. They are easier and faster to build due to prefabricated guideways, are slicker and therefore visually less obtrusive, and may offer easier maintenance.

As Sound Transit is facing escalating construction costs and feels it cannot accommodate traditional elevated trains downtown, it may be a good time to evaluate these and other alternative transit modes. Monorail systems have opened in Bangkok, and TSB has built a maglev test line in China and is looking at several options in Germany. Swyft Cities (working with Whoosh Solutions) and Ottobahn are working on cabins which hang from a guideway like the Wuppertaler Schwebebahn and provide personal rapid transit (PRT).

Similar to a Waymo or Zoox robotaxi, Swyft Cities and Ottobahn offer more route flexibility, are called via phone app, and have small individual cabins with an electric motor. Unlike a robotaxi, they use airspace and don’t get stuck in traffic, they are confined to its track network, have specific parking/staging areas, use electric motors with track power, and use small stations. While Swyft cabins travel on fixed cables (similar to a gondola or the RopeTaxi but those are propelled by the cable), Ottobahn cabins travel on regular tracks at 37mph. For longer distances Ottobahn claims up to 150mph. Both use track switches to guide cabins to their destination.

Ottobahn cabins hang off a bogie which is powered by an electric motor with regular wheels and steel tracks. Cabins either stop at elevated stations or can employ a lift mechanism which drops the cabin to the sidewalk for on- and off-boarding. Ottobahn claims they can support 6000 riders per hour in each direction, or even more with a favorable network design. Similar to a monorail, their track is supported by towers about 120ft apart and between 15 and 30ft high. The track can also cross longer distances over rivers and other obstacles akin to a suspension bridge. Cabins can usually climb up to 7%, with extra support even 12%. That may allow a ship canal crossing.
Swyft is hoping to start projects in Queenstown, Miami, or Los Angeles. Ottobahn started construction of its first network in Phuket .

Traditional train lines serve stations along a linear corridor. Turning a train around at the end of the line takes time as the operator usually has to switch from one end of the train to the other. Lines may branch towards the outer area of a network, but that splits the headway on each branch. As automated train systems do not need to worry about a driver, they can switch direction more easily and offer a bit more flexibility. For example, they can serve short stub lines by backing in and out, though that may impact travel time. PRT systems are not bound to any fixed line/schedule, can use a more elaborate track network, branch on demand, skip stations, and only stop as necessary. Though each cabin may be smaller, short headways may still allow for sufficient capacity.

Any of these systems promise simpler/faster guideway and station construction, easier integration into the existing urban infrastructure, more flexible branching capabilities, and more convenience for riders. It may be worthwhile to consider them for West Seattle or Ballard and other future lines.

articles.title: Seattle Street Ends: Eastlake
articles.author: John Feit (Guest Contributor)
paras: Today we will visit eight street ends and one park in the Eastlake neighborhood. In previous posts, we have looked at street ends around West Seattle , South Ship Canal , from Ballard to Fremont , from Fremont to Portage Bay , as well as the Duwamish Waterway . The last post was for South Lake Union's street ends .

For those new to this series, a little background on Seattle’s Shoreline Street Ends is helpful. Because Seattle is bounded and divided by numerous fresh and salt bodies of water the city has what are called ‘street ends’ — streets that end when they encounter a water body often continue under the water, sometimes resulting in mini-parks or recreational spaces. There are hundreds of such occurrences – almost as many as there are east-west and north-south streets.
Many of them, 142 to be exact, are part of a Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) program called Shoreline Street Ends. The program’s goals are to:

A little over half of the 142 street ends are defined by SDOT as “worth a visit,” while the remainder are either “not yet ready for visitors” or have “no public access.” Street ends are concentrated along the Ship Canal and Lake Washington, but also occur along each of the city’s other shorelines. Working with the city and neighborhoods to secure funding, pass legislation, and organize work parties, the non-profit and all-volunteer Friends of Street Ends help ensure Seattle’s accessible street ends grow in number and those already serving visitors continue to thrive.

Shoreline Street Ends vary in character from sandy beaches to docks wedged amongst shipyards and industrial uses. They are spacious and they are compact, and most are very easy to find. They support habitat for native species of flora and fauna and are convenient places to launch a kayak, sailboat, or motorboat. Oftentimes, they are adjacent to waterfront parks, expanding upon those assets. They are as varied as Seattle’s topography, and you can visit them any time.
Cycling is the best way to visit Seattle’s shoreline street ends. Many are accessed from low-traffic streets or bike paths.

Sitting beneath the Interstate 5 Ship Canal Bridge is the Furman Street street end. A fairly simple affair, it has a broad grass lawn leading to the water and a view towards the University of Washington campus and the several new highrises emerging in its neighborhood. Along Fuhrman and next to the street end is a rowing club, adding a nice buzz of activity.

WSDOT has closed the area off between the rowing club and the street end due to some hazards associated with falling debris from the underside of the bridge while it undergoes repairs. This condition will remain for some time until all necessary repairs are made. That being said it’s still worth a peek.

Partly sandy beach and partly forested landscape, the Martin Street street end can appear mysterious when viewed from Fairview Avenue due to its dense tree canopy and deep shadows. Probing beyond the shadows, however, one can find a waterfront bathed in sunlight. When I visited I happened upon a festive gathering that expanded my appreciation of street ends to be about more than water access and places to catch a view of the water to include unique social and gathering places. Residents from recent apartment development in the neighborhood have added new energy to what used to be a more isolated street end.
SDOT recently finished $375,000 in improvements (most done after these photos were taken). Even if you’ve previously visited the street end, here is a good reason to go again.

The most improved of Eastlake’s street ends, and among the most improved of those I have visited, is the East Allison Street street end. Although lacking the shelter and intimacy of East Martin Street, its staging area for watercraft, generous steps leading to the shoreline, and ADA accessible parking, make it very user friendly.
Right across from the street end is a new neighborhood corner coffee shop, adding a nice amenity to an otherwise desirable location.

East Hamlin Street combines many of the endearing features of Seattle’s street ends, albeit in rustic packaging. It provides a fantastic prospect for viewing Gas Works Park and an intimate lagoon with a sandy shoreline. Other amenities include park benches, a picnic table, as well as an ever changing assortment of lawn chairs along the waterline. The plantings include rose bushes, seagrasses, and a variety of other flora I’m ill equipped to identify. I especially liked the large deciduous trees hovering along its northern edge, their hues changing to golden in the fall day’s crisp air.

Things have been a little tidied up since I took these photos. The paths have new gravel and the benches were repaired, and the neighborhood stewards have done a great job improving and keeping the plantings looking great.

South of East Hamlin Street is East Edgar Street. Although not (yet) part of the Street End program, the Seattle Parks Foundation has information on potential improvements that you can learn more about.

Situated at the tail end of one of Eastlake’s few east-west arterials, Roanoke Street can be hard to miss despite its strategic location and generous amenities. If one looks beyond the parking area along its eastern edge, one finds new street furniture and a paved plaza.

Just to the north is a densely packed, and very urban collection of houseboats. Unlike other neighboring houseboat communities, those along Mallard Cove are arranged parallel to the shoreline giving them a density different from neighboring houseboat communities. This effect is further enhanced by the hillside buildings’ eastern edge.
Boeing’s first factory was located at the foot of Roanoke street.

Unique among the dozens of street ends I visited in the past, Louisa Street has a bocce court and a color theme, whose red brilliance was enhanced by the crimson trees hovering above its like-colored furniture when I visited in the fall.

Neighbors are calling it the Louisa Street Beach since children are having fun playing games in the sand. The two trees to the north have mulch and edging to keep users off the tree roots and we will do additional planting this Fall. This park gets lots of kayak use - a self-service rental is across the street. It also generally has someone simply sitting there and enjoying the day—in all kinds of weather.

Lynn Street Mini Park has a range of amenities and terrific views. Its sandy shoreline is a favorite launching spot for kayakers, and its generously furnished street level terrace allows one to glance above the water enthusiasts to Lake Union. Framed by houseboats to the south and a rare over the water condominium to the north, the park provides one of the more unique and beloved edges along the lake. Although not part of SDOT’s Street End program, and officially a Seattle City Park, its designation matters not for appreciating its fine qualities.

The East Boston Street street end is easily missed unless one has a map in hand. The street end itself is really just the sidewalk along Fairview Avenue – there is no access to the water. Instead, and if one picks just the right viewing angle to snatch a view between the heavily vegetated shoreline one is surprised to see a picturesque assembly of houseboats framing a view across the lake to Queen Anne.

East Newton Street, also known as Terry Pettus Park , is currently undergoing renovation. Prior to its being closed I was able to visit it on a fine fall day in 2023. This particular street end, at least prior to its renovation, had that rarest of amenities: a dock. The dock not only allows one a different way to access the water but it also provides a view back to the shoreline.

It is hard to pick a favorite among the many great street ends along Eastlake Avenue, but Newton Street would certainly be a contender. All construction permits for the renovation have been obtained and I’m sure the neighborhood eagerly awaits its reopening. Click here for project updates.

articles.title: National ground stop response highlights critical errors in public reassurance – saying ‘nothing nefarious’ did the opposite of quelling public concern
articles.author:
<name>Shannon A. Bowen, Professor of Journalism and Mass Communications, University of South Carolina</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/shannon-a-bowen-766905"/>
paras: Thousands of travelers were stranded on Nov. 13, 2026, when the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all domestic flights in the U.S. because of what they said were failures in decades-old air traffic communications systems . Crisis communications expert Shannon A. Bowen , a scholar at the University of South Carolina’s College of Information and Communications, spoke with The Conversation’s Politics and Legal Affairs Editor, Naomi Schalit, about how the Trump administration handled the first day of the crisis.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Is there a first principle in crisis communications?

The first principle would be to react quickly and react with accuracy, react with everything you know at the moment, truthfully, but always react quickly. Because if you delay until you gather information, a vacuum will ensue. Information fills that vacuum that may not be accurate. And so that’s the enemy of accurate crisis communication, but you want to always speak quickly and be the most authoritative and definitive source, even if very little information is known.
What did we see on the day of the ground stop?

A crisis unfolded and to the administration’s credit, they did react very quickly , in a way that offered the information that was known at the time, even though not a lot was known about why the ground stop was issued until later.
You’re speaking about the short press conference that afternoon with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin?

He did keep saying that nothing nefarious was at hand . And for a crisis communication scholar, you would not want to introduce the idea that something nefarious was at hand, unless, indeed, something nefarious was at hand. So by the very act of introducing this concept and this idea, I think the talking point, “Nothing nefarious,” then went across multiple networks, and it became the center of a controversy rather than quelling a controversy.

By saying nothing nefarious is at hand, that indeed confirmed something nefarious was at hand, even if the nefariousness was only the mismanagement of the air traffic control systems routers that they claimed caused the problem. By introducing this idea, I believe it did bring to mind that there may be other state actors behind whatever happened, that it could be a cyber attack. It would have been better to say, “We have evidence that this was not a cyber attack but a hardware failure.”
How did the later press conference with Mullin and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy go from your perspective as an expert on crisis communications?
They handled the questions that they received correctly. They told us as much information as they knew.
However, they did seem to downplay the extent of this crisis, because we have to remember the traveling public is not just people trying to get to business meetings.

We had football teams stranded. Now football Saturday , all over the SEC, has been disrupted. And there’s probably disruption in other areas of the country, but to us in the South, SEC football is almost a religious experience on Saturday . Luckily, the University of South Carolina football team had already flown out . But our marching band was stuck in this crisis, and so we have a lot of ripple effects from something like this happening, and it definitely says to me that this was an emergency situation. It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale.

If it were simply routers being overloaded, as we’ve been told, why wouldn’t they already know this situation and restart those routers the night before or over Friday night after most of the traveling public is out of the air?
What was Mullin’s and Duffy’s job when they got out there? What did they need to do?

To inform the public about the danger, why this happened, the extent of the problem, and what they’re doing to remediate the problem. We keep hearing that they’re asking for US$30 billion and more to repair the whole infrastructure for the air traffic control system, which is great, but what are they doing right now?

How do we know that flights in the air, right this minute, are any safer than the ones yesterday, a minute before the ground stop? Do we have that information? I don’t feel confident that they addressed that question appropriately. I don’t think that the traveling public entirely feels safe at this point or adequately informed that they will arrive at their destination.
They introduced politics into the press conference as well, didn’t they?

It’s something that they have the prerogative to do. They are both political appointees and members of the cabinet . So I understand that aspect, but I really wish they had addressed the traveling public’s concerns more overtly before making it political, that they need more money to fix this. We know they need more money to fix it, and I’m sure the American taxpayers are aware of the problem and willing to fund those corrections. But the more expedient issues would be, what about all these people who were stuck in airports ?
Were there warning signs for this crisis?

I believe there were. We had another ground stop about three years ago , due to air traffic control problems, and that is what we call in crisis communications a “prodrome ,” a warning sign of larger impending problems. When you see these types of warning signs, it really gives us a reason to think it’s going to get worse.

Duffy did say on Nov. 13 that, because of the condition of the air traffic infrastructure, “ you will have more ” ground stoppages. If you had a piece of advice for the administration regarding their future communications, what would you tell them?

I would say to communicate in advance as much as possible, so if you’re even considering a ground stop, it may be a good idea to put out a public notice so that people don’t go to the airport on a vacation flight, maybe they delay that for a week or two. It might also be a good idea to speak with the airline industry representatives and say, “Here’s what we’re thinking. Can you work with us? How can we make this better for the traveling public?” Also, if 17 of 22 routers were malfunctioning, could we have had a partial ground stop at only the affected airports, rather than a nationwide stop?
My silly last question: Do crisis communications experts have any theories about Friday the 13th?

We consider it more of a superstition, but I have noticed that there does tend to be a lot of activity on Friday the 13th. It might be placebo effect, it might be because we expect something bad to happen and we’re looking for it. But that day does seem to always have some type of activity. This is also when organizations release bad news, oftentimes, they say, “Let’s hold it until Friday the 13th, because bad news is expected.” People will assume, on Friday the 13th, that negative things are going to come out, so the shock value won’t be as much.
Shannon A. Bowen received funding in 2022-2023 from The National Science Foundation as PI on a grant studying disaster management.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Cascadia High-Speed Rail and I-5
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: To plan the next generation of north-south travel in western Washington, the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) is working on the I-5 Master Plan and the Cascadia High Speed Rail project. These two projects have been integrated into a combined Cascaida Program . WSDOT is asking for your feedback on what should be prioritized as the program progresses. The survey closes tonight so be sure to fill it out today.

The Cascadia Program is focused on the transportation of people and goods between Portland, Seattle, and Vancouver (BC). While this corridor crosses two states and an international boarder, 88% of the route is located in Washington. As a result, WSDOT is leading the effort while working with agencies in Oregon and British Columbia.

The survey asks about how and why you travel throughout the megaregion today as well as your priorities for I-5 and HSR.
